title: Nazar Amulet Emoji 🧿 Meaning: The Evil Eye Charm
description: The 🧿 nazar amulet emoji is the blue evil eye bead. Learn what it protects against, why people add it to good news, and how it differs from the hamsa.
summary: The 🧿 nazar amulet emoji shows the blue glass bead used across Turkey, Greece and the Middle East to deflect the evil eye. People post it for protection: next to good news, baby photos, new ventures or compliments, as a way of saying “no jinx, no jealousy.”
meaning: The bead in this emoji is a nazar, a charm of concentric blue, white and black circles that looks like an eye staring back. The belief behind it is old and widespread: an envious or admiring look can bring bad luck, and the bead meets that look so the wearer doesn't have to. In Turkey it is called a nazar boncuğu and hangs in doorways, cars, shops and on babies' clothing. Greeks know the same idea as the mati.

Online, the emoji does the job the physical bead does. Someone announces a promotion, shows off a new apartment or posts a happy couple photo and adds 🧿 to guard the moment from envy. It works like knocking on wood, except it is aimed at other people's eyes rather than at fate. Friends drop it in the comments under good news as a blessing, often alongside a compliment so the praise itself doesn't jinx anything.

A second, looser use grew out of wellness and astrology accounts, where 🧿 sits next to crystals and moons as a general symbol of protected energy and boundaries. Captions like “protecting my peace 🧿” come from that world. Some users simply like the look of it and use it as a blue aesthetic accent, with no belief attached.

People sometimes call this emoji “the evil eye,” but strictly speaking it is the opposite: the evil eye is the harmful glance, and the nazar is the defense against it. For many users from Turkish, Greek, Arab, Persian, South Asian and Sephardic backgrounds it is a familiar household object and a small marker of heritage.

contexts.label: In captions
contexts.body: The classic placement is at the end of a post that shares something enviable: a graduation, a pregnancy announcement, a new car, a business opening. It signals gratitude plus caution. Many people use it alone as the entire caption under a photo they are proud of, which reads as “blessed, and keeping it that way.”

contexts.label: In comments and replies
contexts.body: Replying 🧿 to a friend's good news means “may nothing spoil this.” It is common under baby photos and wedding pictures, where in many cultures a bare compliment is considered risky. Paired with “mashallah” it is a standard response among Muslim users to anything beautiful or fortunate.

contexts.label: In bios and usernames
contexts.body: A 🧿 in a profile bio usually says the account owner is guarding their energy from haters, or points to roots in a culture where the bead is everywhere. On spiritual, tarot and manifestation accounts it is part of the standard decoration alongside the crystal ball and the hamsa.

contexts.label: Around the world
contexts.body: The symbol is most at home around the Mediterranean, the Balkans, the Middle East and Central and South Asia, and it travels with those diasporas. Tourists know it as the souvenir sold in every Turkish and Greek market. Elsewhere, many people first met it as jewelry and use the emoji mainly as a fashion or good-vibes symbol.

examples.text: Got the keys to our first home today 🧿
examples.meaning: Sharing big news while warding off jealousy or bad luck.
Praising a child and adding protection so the compliment doesn't jinx her.

examples.text: Not telling anyone about the new job until I sign 🧿
examples.meaning: Keeping plans quiet so nothing goes wrong before it's official.
Setting boundaries and shutting out negativity.

examples.text: Picked this up at the Grand Bazaar 🧿
examples.meaning: A literal reference to buying a nazar bead as a souvenir.

combos.meaning: Double protection: the nazar bead plus the hamsa hand, both charms against the evil eye.
Good energy only; a blessed moment the poster wants kept safe.
Grateful for good fortune and praying it lasts.
A baby photo or announcement shielded from envious looks.

confusedWith.difference: The 🪬 hamsa is an open hand, often with an eye in the palm, used by Jewish, Muslim and other Middle Eastern and North African communities. Both ward off the evil eye; the nazar is the round blue bead on its own.
The 👁️ eye is a realistic human eye used for watching, seeing or staring. It carries no protective meaning, while 🧿 is a stylized charm that only resembles an eye.
The 🔵 blue circle is a plain colored dot used for bullet points, team colors or status markers. At small sizes the two look similar, but the nazar has white and dark rings inside.

avoid: Don't send it to mean you are giving someone the evil eye; it protects against the glance rather than delivering one.
Skip it as a joke about superstition when talking with people for whom the nazar is a sincere family tradition.
design: Every major platform draws a round, flat bead made of concentric circles: a dark blue outer ring, then white, then light blue, with a black dot at the center like a pupil. Shades of blue and the thickness of the rings vary slightly, and some versions add a glassy highlight, but the design is consistent enough that it reads the same everywhere.

faqs.q: Is the 🧿 emoji the evil eye?
faqs.a: Not exactly. The evil eye is the curse, an envious glance believed to cause harm. The 🧿 is the nazar, the amulet that deflects it. Calling the emoji “the evil eye” is common shorthand, but its meaning is protective.

faqs.q: What does 🧿 mean in someone's bio?
faqs.a: It usually means the person wants protection from envy and negativity, or it signals cultural roots in a place where the bead is traditional, such as Turkey or Greece. On spiritual accounts it marks an interest in energy and protection.

faqs.q: Is it disrespectful to use the nazar emoji if I'm not from that culture?
faqs.a: The symbol is shared by many cultures and religions and is sold freely as jewelry and souvenirs, so casual use is widely accepted. Using it to mock the belief is where people take offense.
The nazar amulet arrived in 2018 as part of Emoji 11.0. Before that, people often substituted a blue circle or an eye emoji to suggest the charm.

faqs.q: What does it mean when someone comments 🧿 on my photo?
faqs.a: They are wishing you well. The comment says your news or your picture is good enough to attract envy, and they want it kept safe. Treat it as a compliment with a blessing attached.
